learning_objective: 🎯 Master the FIFO (First-In-First-Out) linear data structure, its variants (Circular Queue, Deque), and its role in scheduling and resource buffering.

key_vocabulary.definition: First-In, First-Out: The principle governing queues where the oldest added item is removed first.
The operation of adding an element to the Rear (end) of the queue.
The operation of removing an element from the Front (head) of the queue.
Front is the pointer where deletions occur; Rear is the pointer where insertions occur.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A queue works like a line at a ticket counter. Elements join at the Rear (Enqueue) and leave from the Front (Dequeue). In Python lists, `.append(item)` adds to the rear and `.pop(0)` removes from the front.

In a fixed-array queue, empty spaces left by dequeued items at the front are wasted. A Circular Queue connects the rear end back to the front position (`(Rear + 1) % SIZE`), reusing empty spaces efficiently.
A Deque (pronounced 'deck') allows insertions and deletions from both ends (Front and Rear). It can act as either a Stack or a Queue depending on how operations are restricted.
Queues are used wherever resources must be shared fairly: 1) Printer job spooling, 2) CPU task scheduling in operating systems, 3) Call center routing, and 4) Breadth-First Search (BFS) in graphs.

exam_tips: 📌 When implementing queues with standard Python lists, remember that `.pop(0)` takes $O(n)$ time because all remaining elements shift left.
📌 For a Circular Queue of size `N`, the queue is Full when `(Rear + 1) % N == Front`, and Empty when `Front == -1`.
📌 Don't confuse 'Deque' (Double-Ended Queue) with 'Dequeue' (the operation of removing an item from a queue).
quick_recap: ⭐ The `collections.deque` module in Python provides $O(1)$ time complexity for appends and pops from both ends (`appendleft` / `popleft`).
⭐ A Priority Queue is a special queue where elements are dequeued based on their assigned priority value rather than arrival time.
⭐ Queues handle asynchronous data transfer between two processes operating at different speeds (e.g., IO buffers).
